Galatians calls us to boast only “in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14).

For reflection

What do you tend to add to Christ as a way of feeling right with God?

49.title: Ephesians: Blessed in Christ
49.essay:
Ephesians soars. It begins with every spiritual blessing that God has given his people in Christ, and moves to the church, one new humanity of Jews and Gentiles, and how it should live.

Setting

Paul wrote from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62. It may have been a circular letter for several churches around Ephesus.

Outline

1–3 · What God has done. God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, redeemed us through his blood and sealed us with the Spirit. We were dead in sin, but “by grace you have been saved through faith” (Ephesians 2:8). Jews and Gentiles are now one body. Paul prays that they may know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge.

4–6 · How we should live. Walk worthy of your calling, in unity, holiness and love. Wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters, live as those who belong to Christ. Put on the whole armour of God.

The armour of God

Paul’s armour (Ephesians 6:10–18) is not a set of techniques, but the gospel itself applied: the truth that holds everything together, the righteousness of Christ given to us and lived out, the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace, faith that trusts God’s promises when the enemy attacks, the assurance of salvation guarding the mind, and the word of God, the only offensive weapon, all taken up in prayer.

Christ in Ephesians

The phrase “in Christ” and its equivalents appear again and again. Everything God gives, he gives in Christ, and everything will be united in him (Ephesians 1:10).

For worship

Ephesians opens with praise: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing” (Ephesians 1:3).

For reflection

Read Ephesians 1:3–14. Which blessing in Christ do you most need to remember today?

50.title: Philippians: Joy in Christ
50.essay:
Written from prison, Philippians is full of joy. Paul thanks the church for their partnership, urges them to humility and unity after the pattern of Christ, and teaches the secret of contentment.

Setting

Paul wrote from prison, probably in Rome, around AD 61–62, to the first church he planted in Europe.

Outline

1 · Partnership and imprisonment. Paul rejoices that his chains have advanced the gospel. “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21).

2 · The mind of Christ. Paul calls them to humility, quoting what may be an early hymn: Christ, though in the form of God, emptied himself, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death on a cross, and God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:5–11).

3 · Knowing Christ. Paul counts all his former privileges as loss “because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8).

4 · Peace and contentment. “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Philippians 4:4). Pray instead of being anxious. Paul has learnt contentment in every situation: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13).

What it does not mean

Philippians 4:13 is not a promise that you can achieve any goal you set. In context, Paul means that through Christ he can be content in hunger or plenty, in prison or freedom.

Christ in Philippians

Philippians 2 is one of the greatest passages on the humiliation and exaltation of Christ, before whom every knee will bow.

For worship

Philippians shows that joy does not depend on circumstances, but on Christ.

For reflection

What is threatening your joy at the moment? How does knowing Christ change it?

51.title: Colossians: Christ Is All
51.essay:
False teaching at Colossae suggested that Christ was not enough, and that believers needed extra knowledge, rules or spiritual experiences. Paul answers by showing the supremacy and sufficiency of Christ.

Setting

Written from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62, to a church Paul had not visited, founded by Epaphras.

Outline

1 · The supremacy of Christ. “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. For by him all things were created” (Colossians 1:15–16). He is the head of the church, and through his blood God has reconciled all things.

2 · The sufficiency of Christ. “For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him” (Colossians 2:9–10). Do not be taken captive by philosophy, rules about food and festivals, or the worship of angels. Christ disarmed the powers at the cross.

3–4 · Life in Christ. Set your minds on things above. Put off the old self and put on the new. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly. Christ is Lord in the home and at work.

Christ in Colossians

Christ is the Creator, the sustainer of all things, the head of the church and the firstborn from the dead. “Christ is all, and in all” (Colossians 3:11).

For worship

Colossians lifts our eyes to a Christ so great that nothing could ever be added to him.

For reflection

Is there anything you are looking to, alongside Christ, to make you complete?

52.title: 1 Thessalonians: Waiting for the Son from Heaven
52.essay:
A young church, persecuted soon after Paul was forced to leave, needed encouragement. Paul thanks God for their faith, urges them to holiness, and comforts them about believers who have died, with the hope of Christ’s return.

Setting

One of Paul’s earliest letters, written from Corinth around AD 50–51.

Outline

1–3 · Thanksgiving and concern. The Thessalonians “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven” (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10). Paul recalls his gentle ministry among them and rejoices at Timothy’s good report.

4–5 · Living and waiting. Live in holiness and love, and work quietly. Do not grieve as those without hope: the dead in Christ will rise first when the Lord descends from heaven (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). The day of the Lord will come like a thief, so stay awake. “Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances” (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18).

Christ in 1 Thessalonians

Christ died for us, “so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him” (1 Thessalonians 5:10). He is coming again.

For worship

The hope of Christ’s return comforts the grieving and motivates holy living.

For reflection

How does the promise that the dead in Christ will rise change the way you grieve?

53.title: 2 Thessalonians: Stand Firm
53.essay:
Some in Thessalonica were confused, thinking the day of the Lord had already come, and some had stopped working. Paul corrects their misunderstanding and urges them to stand firm and work.

Setting

Written from Corinth soon after 1 Thessalonians, around AD 51.

Outline

1 · Comfort in persecution. God will judge their persecutors and give rest to the afflicted when Christ is revealed from heaven.

2 · The day of the Lord. That day will not come until the rebellion and the man of lawlessness are revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will destroy. Stand firm in the traditions you were taught.

3 · Work and pray. Pray for the spread of the word. Keep away from idleness: “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

Different views

Christians have understood the man of lawlessness in different ways: a final individual antichrist, a recurring principle of opposition, or (as many Reformers held) the papacy. Paul’s main point is clear whichever view is taken: do not be shaken by claims about the end, and keep living faithfully.

Christ in 2 Thessalonians

The Lord Jesus will come in glory to be “marveled at among all who have believed” (2 Thessalonians 1:10).

For worship

2 Thessalonians gives stability in confusing times: Christ will win, and his people are safe.

For reflection

Are speculations about the end times distracting you from faithful, ordinary work?

54.title: 1 Timothy: Conduct in God’s Household
54.essay:
Paul writes to Timothy, his young colleague leading the church in Ephesus, to guard sound doctrine, order the church’s life and qualify its leaders, so that people may know “how one ought to behave in the household of God” (1 Timothy 3:15).

Setting

Written around AD 62–64, after Paul’s release from his first Roman imprisonment.

Outline

1 · Sound doctrine. Stop false teachers. Paul remembers his own conversion: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost” (1 Timothy 1:15).

2–3 · Worship and leaders. Pray for all people, for God desires all to be saved. Instructions for men and women in worship, and qualifications for elders and deacons.

4 · Godliness. Avoid false asceticism. Train yourself for godliness. “Let no one despise you for your youth” (1 Timothy 4:12).

5–6 · Caring for the church. Instructions about widows, elders and slaves. Godliness with contentment is great gain, but the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. Fight the good fight of faith.

Christ in 1 Timothy

“For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:5–6).

For worship

1 Timothy bursts into praise: “To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever” (1 Timothy 1:17).

For reflection

Are you training yourself in godliness as seriously as some train their bodies?

55.title: 2 Timothy: Guard the Deposit
55.essay:
2 Timothy is Paul’s last letter, written from a Roman prison shortly before his execution. He urges Timothy to guard the gospel, suffer for it, and preach the word.

Setting

Written around AD 64–67, during Paul’s final imprisonment.

Outline

1 · Do not be ashamed. Fan into flame the gift of God. Guard the good deposit entrusted to you.

2 · Endure. Entrust the teaching to faithful men who will teach others. Suffer like a good soldier. Rightly handle the word of truth.

3 · Continue in Scripture. Difficult times will come. “All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16).

4 · Preach the word. “Preach the word; be ready in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2). Paul is ready to die: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7).

Christ in 2 Timothy

Christ “abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10). “If we are faithless, he remains faithful” (2 Timothy 2:13).

For worship

2 Timothy shows a man facing death with confidence, because he knows whom he has believed.

For reflection

To whom are you passing on the faith, as Paul did to Timothy?

56.title: Titus: Sound Doctrine and Good Works
56.essay:
Paul left Titus in Crete to appoint elders and set the churches in order. Crete was known for dishonesty, and Paul stresses that sound doctrine must produce godly lives.

Setting

Written around AD 62–64, between Paul’s imprisonments.

Outline

1 · Elders. Appoint elders who are above reproach, able to teach sound doctrine and refute those who oppose it.

2 · Teaching for every group. Instructions for older men and women, younger men and women, and slaves, so that they may “adorn the doctrine of God our Savior” (Titus 2:10). The grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness as we wait for the appearing of Christ.

3 · Good works. Be ready for every good work. God saved us “not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5).

Christ in Titus

Titus 2:13 calls Christ “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ”, a clear statement of his deity, “who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness” (Titus 2:14).

For worship

Titus shows that grace not only saves us but trains us, and makes us a people zealous for good works.

For reflection

Does your life adorn the gospel, making it attractive to others?

57.title: Philemon: Receive Him as You Would Me
57.essay:
Philemon is a short personal letter about a runaway slave, Onesimus, who had become a Christian through Paul. Paul sends him back to his master, asking Philemon to receive him “no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16).

Setting

Written from prison around AD 60–62, sent with the letter to the Colossians.

Outline

1–7 · Thanksgiving. Paul thanks God for Philemon’s love and faith.

8–20 · The appeal. Paul appeals, rather than commands, for Onesimus. “If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account” (Philemon 18).

21–25 · Confidence and greetings. Paul is confident Philemon will do even more than he asks.

Philemon and slavery

Paul does not directly attack the institution of slavery here. But by calling master and slave brothers, equal in Christ, he plants a principle that undermines it. Later Christians, like Wilberforce, drew on such truths in the fight against slavery.

Christ in Philemon

Paul’s offer to pay Onesimus’s debt is a picture of Christ, who took our debt on himself and presents us to the Father as his own.

For worship

Philemon shows the gospel reconciling people across the deepest social divides.

For reflection

Is there someone you need to welcome back as a brother or sister, because Christ has welcomed you?

58.title: Hebrews: Jesus Is Better
58.essay:
Hebrews was written to Jewish Christians tempted to turn back to the old ways under persecution. Its message: Jesus is better than angels, Moses, the priesthood and the sacrifices. So do not drift away; hold fast to him.

Setting

The author is unknown. Paul, Barnabas, Apollos and others have been suggested. It was probably written before the temple’s destruction in AD 70.

Outline

1–2 · Better than angels. God has spoken finally in his Son, who is “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature” (Hebrews 1:3). He became human to destroy death and help us.

3–4 · Better than Moses. Moses was a servant in God’s house; Christ is the Son over it. Do not harden your hearts, but enter God’s rest.

5–10 · A better priest and sacrifice. Christ is a high priest after the order of Melchizedek, mediator of a better covenant. He offered himself “once for all” (Hebrews 10:10), and sat down at God’s right hand.

11–13 · Faith and endurance. A great cloud of witnesses lived by faith. So run the race, “looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2).

The warning passages

Hebrews warns sternly against falling away (Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–31). Christians differ on how to read these. Some say true believers can lose their salvation. The Reformed view, which fits the whole of Scripture best, is that the warnings describe people who tasted the blessings of the gospel without being truly born again, and that God uses such warnings to keep his true people persevering (Hebrews 6:9).

Christ in Hebrews

The whole book is about Christ: Son, Creator, priest, sacrifice and King.

For worship

Hebrews calls us to draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, because our great high priest sympathises with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15–16).

For reflection

What are you tempted to go back to, instead of holding fast to Christ?

59.title: James: Faith That Works
59.essay:
James is practical and direct. It insists that real faith shows itself in action: in trials, in speech, in care for the poor, in humility and in patience. “Faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead” (James 2:17).

Setting

Written by James, the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church, probably in the 40s AD, making it one of the earliest New Testament books.

Outline

1 · Trials and the word. Count it all joy when you meet trials. Ask God for wisdom. Be doers of the word, not hearers only.

2 · Faith and works. Do not show favouritism to the rich. Faith without works is dead.

3 · The tongue. The tongue is a small fire that can set a forest ablaze. True wisdom is pure and peaceable.

4–5 · Humility and patience. Submit to God, resist the devil. Do not boast about tomorrow. Woe to the oppressive rich. Be patient until the Lord comes, and pray for one another.

James and Paul

Do James and Paul contradict each other? No. Paul says we are justified by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28), meaning works do not earn our acceptance before God. James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (James 2:24), meaning that true faith is shown to be real by its works. As the Reformers said, we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

Christ in James

James calls himself “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (James 1:1), and much of the letter echoes Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount.

For worship

James shows that worship is not only songs, but a life: “Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world” (James 1:27).

For reflection

Where is your faith not yet showing itself in action?

60.title: 1 Peter: Hope for Exiles
60.essay:
Peter writes to Christians scattered across Asia Minor who were suffering for their faith. He calls them “elect exiles” and gives them a living hope, a new identity and a pattern for suffering well.

Setting

Written by Peter from “Babylon”, probably Rome, around AD 62–64, shortly before Nero’s persecution.

Outline

1:1–2:10 · A new identity. God has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus. Be holy. You are “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9).

2:11–4:11 · Living as exiles. Live honourably among unbelievers. Submit to authorities, masters and husbands, following the pattern of Christ, who suffered without retaliating. Be ready to give a reason for your hope.

4:12–5:14 · Suffering and glory. Do not be surprised at fiery trials. Elders, shepherd the flock. “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6). Resist the devil.

A difficult passage

1 Peter 3:18–20 says Christ “went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison.” This is one of the hardest texts in the New Testament. Some think Christ preached through Noah to his generation; others that after his death he proclaimed victory to fallen spirits. It does not teach a second chance after death. The most likely view is a proclamation of triumph.

Christ in 1 Peter

“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). He is the cornerstone, the shepherd and overseer of our souls, and the pattern for our suffering.

For worship

1 Peter fixes our hope on an inheritance that is “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4).

For reflection

How does knowing you are an exile, with a home in heaven, change the way you face suffering?

61.title: 2 Peter: Grow in Grace
61.essay:
In his last letter, Peter warns against false teachers who deny Christ’s return and live immorally. He calls believers to grow in grace and knowledge, trusting the sure word of God.

Setting

Peter wrote shortly before his death, around AD 64–67. Its authorship has been questioned since early times, but the church received it as from Peter.

Outline

1 · Growth and the sure word. God has given us everything we need for life and godliness. Add to your faith virtue, knowledge, self-control and love. Peter saw Christ’s glory at the transfiguration, and Scripture came as “men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21).

2 · False teachers. They will bring destructive heresies and exploit people with greed and sensuality. God knows how to rescue the godly and judge the wicked.

3 · The day of the Lord. Scoffers will mock the promise of his coming. But God is patient, “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). The day will come, and we wait for new heavens and a new earth.

Christ in 2 Peter

Peter calls him “our God and Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Peter 1:1). He ends: “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity” (2 Peter 3:18).

For worship

2 Peter teaches us to see God’s patience as mercy, and to live holy lives as we wait for his day.

For reflection

In which of Peter’s qualities, virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection or love, do you most need to grow?

62.title: 1 John: That You May Know
62.essay:
John writes to churches shaken by false teachers who had left them. He gives tests of true faith, so that believers may have assurance: “I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13).

Setting

Written by the apostle John, probably from Ephesus, around AD 85–95.

Outline

The letter circles around three tests, returning to them several times.

The test of truth. True believers confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. Those who deny the Son do not have the Father.

The test of obedience. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). Those who know God keep his commandments and do not make a practice of sin.

The test of love. “Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God” (1 John 4:7). Whoever does not love does not know God, “because God is love” (1 John 4:8).

A textual note

Some older English Bibles include at 1 John 5:7–8 a statement about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit as three witnesses in heaven. This “Johannine Comma” is absent from almost all Greek manuscripts before the sixteenth century and is not original. The doctrine of the Trinity stands firmly on other texts and does not need it.

Christ in 1 John

“In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10).

For worship

1 John fills us with wonder: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God” (1 John 3:1).

For reflection

Which of John’s three tests gives you the most assurance, and which the most challenge?

63.title: 2 John: Truth and Love
63.essay:
A short letter to “the elect lady and her children”, probably a church, urging them to walk in love and truth, and not to welcome teachers who deny that Christ came in the flesh.

Setting

Written by John, who calls himself “the elder”, around the same time as 1 John.

Outline

1–6 · Walk in love. John rejoices that some are walking in the truth, and urges them to love one another, which means walking according to God’s commandments.

7–11 · Beware of deceivers. Many deceivers deny the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Do not receive them or support their work.

12–13 · Closing. John hopes to visit and speak face to face.

Christ in 2 John

The true doctrine of Christ, God come in the flesh, is the dividing line between truth and error. “Whoever abides in the teaching has both the Father and the Son” (2 John 9).

For worship

2 John shows that love and truth belong together. Love without truth is sentiment; truth without love is harshness.

For reflection

Do you lean towards truth without love, or love without truth?

64.title: 3 John: Walking in the Truth
64.essay:
A personal letter to Gaius, praising his hospitality to travelling missionaries, and warning about Diotrephes, a church leader who loves to be first.

Setting

Written by John, “the elder”, around the same time as his other letters.

Outline

1–8 · Gaius. John rejoices that Gaius walks in the truth. “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth” (3 John 4). He commends Gaius’s support of missionaries.

9–10 · Diotrephes. He refuses John’s authority, gossips, and turns away fellow believers.

11–15 · Demetrius and greetings. Imitate good, not evil. Demetrius has a good testimony.

Christ in 3 John

The missionaries went out “for the sake of the name” (3 John 7), the name of Christ. Supporting them makes us “fellow workers for the truth” (3 John 8).

For worship

3 John shows that ordinary hospitality, given for Christ’s sake, is a real share in his mission.

For reflection

Are you more like Gaius, generous and welcoming, or like Diotrephes, wanting to be first?

65.title: Jude: Contend for the Faith
65.essay:
Jude intended to write about salvation, but felt compelled instead to urge believers “to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 3), because ungodly people had crept into the church.

Setting

Written by Jude, the brother of James and of Jesus, probably in the 60s AD.

Outline

1–4 · The purpose. Contend for the faith, because some have perverted the grace of God into sensuality and deny Christ.

5–16 · Examples of judgment. Israel in the wilderness, the angels who sinned, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam and Korah. Jude quotes the book of Enoch about God’s coming judgment.

17–23 · Keep yourselves in God’s love. Build yourselves up in faith, pray in the Spirit, wait for mercy, and have mercy on those who doubt.

24–25 · Doxology. “Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy” (Jude 24).

Jude and other books

Jude quotes 1 Enoch and alludes to a story about Michael and the body of Moses. This does not make those books Scripture, any more than Paul’s quoting of pagan poets made them Scripture (Acts 17:28). Jude uses a true statement from a known source.

Christ in Jude

Believers are “kept for Jesus Christ” (Jude 1), and wait for his mercy that leads to eternal life.

For worship

Jude’s closing doxology is one of the greatest in Scripture: God is able to keep us to the end.

For reflection

How can you contend for the faith while also showing mercy to those who doubt?

66.title: Revelation: The Lamb Who Reigns
66.essay:
Revelation draws back the curtain to show the risen Christ ruling over history, his suffering church, the judgment of evil, and the new creation where God will live with his people for ever.

Setting

Written by John, exiled on Patmos, around AD 95, to seven churches in Asia Minor facing persecution and compromise.

Outline

1–3 · Christ and his churches. John sees the glorified Christ among the lampstands. He sends letters to seven churches, praising, rebuking and promising rewards to those who conquer.

4–5 · The throne and the Lamb. In heaven, all creation worships God on the throne. Only the Lamb who was slain is worthy to open the scroll of history.

6–16 · Seals, trumpets and bowls. Three series of judgments show God’s wrath against a rebellious world, while his people are sealed and protected. The dragon, Satan, wages war through the beast and the false prophet, but the saints conquer “by the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 12:11).

17–20 · The fall of Babylon and the final victory. The great city of human pride falls. Christ rides out as King of kings. Satan is bound and finally thrown into the lake of fire. The dead are judged.

21–22 · The new creation. “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). There is no more death or tears. “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

How to read it

Revelation is apocalyptic and full of symbols, many drawn from the Old Testament. Christians read it in different ways: as mainly about the first century, about the end of history, or as a picture of the whole church age. The app takes the last view, with an amillennial reading of chapter 20, but all agree on its main message: Jesus wins, and his people must stay faithful.

Christ in Revelation

Christ is the Alpha and Omega, the Lion who is the Lamb, the faithful witness, the Bridegroom and the King. The book begins and ends with him.

For worship

Revelation is full of worship. It teaches us to join the song of heaven: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain” (Revelation 5:12).

For reflection

How does knowing how the story ends give you courage for today?
